dimensions.name: Focus on UI work
dimensions.definition: The checklist stays centered on the front-end cosmetic changes and does not drift into broader implementation details.
dimensions.why_it_matters: You want it to focus on the specific UI changes and nothing else when asked to accomplish a task.
dimensions.bad_example: The checklist starts describing general implementation work, backend changes, or broad project status instead of the UI updates that were made.
dimensions.good_example: The checklist names the UI changes and keeps the summary tightly scoped to the front-end work.
dimensions.better_example: The checklist reads like a clean change log for the visual edits and avoids unrelated implementation details.
dimensions.best_example: The checklist only describes the exact cosmetic UI changes that were made, with no drift into broader code or project discussion.

dimensions.name: Clear project or screen reference
dimensions.definition: The checklist identifies the project or screen clearly enough that the change can be tracked later without confusion.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The change needs to be tied to the right work so the reviewer can file and find it easily.
dimensions.bad_example: The checklist leaves out the project or screen entirely, so it is hard to tell what the change belongs to.
dimensions.good_example: The checklist names the project or screen in a way that makes the change easy to track.
dimensions.better_example: The checklist gives enough context to show exactly where the UI change belongs.
dimensions.best_example: The checklist makes the work easy to trace later because the project or screen is clear right away.

dimensions.name: Specific change items
dimensions.definition: Each checklist item says exactly what was changed so a reviewer can tell what actually happened.
dimensions.why_it_matters: If the items are too broad, I can’t tell what was actually done.
dimensions.bad_example: The checklist items are so vague or generic that they could apply to any project and do not show what changed.
dimensions.good_example: The checklist items clearly describe the UI edits that were completed.
dimensions.better_example: The checklist items are specific enough that a reviewer can tell what was updated without guessing.
dimensions.best_example: Each checklist item reads like a faithful record of the front-end work and makes the exact UI changes obvious at a glance.

dimensions.name: Review context and caveats
dimensions.definition: The checklist calls out the important context, constraints, or follow-up notes a reviewer needs to assess the change safely.
dimensions.why_it_matters: It should include anything important I should know for review.
dimensions.bad_example: The checklist skips the caveats or follow-up notes that a reviewer would need to judge the change safely.
dimensions.good_example: The checklist calls out the key context or constraints that matter for review.
dimensions.better_example: The checklist includes the important caveats and follow-up notes without turning into a long explanation.
dimensions.best_example: The checklist surfaces the exact context a reviewer needs so they can approve the change without hunting for missing details.

dimensions.name: Clear follow-up step
dimensions.definition: The checklist ends with an obvious next step for reviewing or checking the result.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The reviewer should have a clear next step for checking the result.
dimensions.bad_example: The checklist ends without telling the reviewer what to check next or how to confirm the change.
dimensions.good_example: The checklist gives a simple next step for reviewing the updated UI.
dimensions.better_example: The checklist points the reviewer to the most relevant place or view to verify the change.
dimensions.best_example: The checklist ends with a clear review step that makes it easy to confirm the UI change right away.
